taglines: Dwarf Galaxy: A small galaxy containing thousands to billions of stars, often orbiting larger galaxies.
Magellanic Clouds: Two companion dwarf galaxies orbiting the Milky Way, clearly visible from the southern sky.
Dark Matter: An invisible form of matter making up most cosmic mass, interacting only through gravity.
Supernova: A colossal stellar explosion marking the dramatic end of a massive star's life cycle.
Nebula: An immense cloud of gas and dust in interstellar space where new stars are born.
Magellanic Stream: A vast trail of hydrogen gas drawn out behind the Magellanic Clouds by gravitational forces.
Magellanic Bridge: A bridge of gas and young stars connecting the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds.
Satellite Galaxy: A smaller galaxy gravitationally bound to and orbiting a larger parent galaxy.
Barred Spiral Galaxy: A spiral galaxy featuring a central bar-shaped structure of stars, like the Milky Way.
Spiral Arm: A winding structure of stars and gas sweeping outward from the core, rich in young stars.
Density Wave: A compression wave traveling through a galaxy disc that compresses gas to ignite star birth.
Galactic Bulge: A tightly packed, spherical group of older stars at the center of a spiral galaxy.
Supermassive Black Hole: A colossal black hole millions to billions of times the Sun's mass at galactic cores.
Galactic Halo: A spherical region enveloping a galactic disc, containing ancient star clusters and dark matter.
Galactic Year: The time taken for the Solar System to orbit the galactic center, about 230 million years.
Ring Galaxy: A galaxy with a brilliant ring of young stars encircling its core, formed by a bullseye collision.
Hoag's Object: An extraordinarily rare ring galaxy with an almost perfect blue ring around a yellow core.
Cartwheel Galaxy: A famous collisional ring galaxy displaying spoke-like structures connecting core to rim.
Globular Cluster: A dense spherical cluster of hundreds of thousands of ancient stars bound by gravity.
Local Group: The galactic group containing the Milky Way, Andromeda, Triangulum, and over 80 dwarf galaxies.

chapterTaglines.1: The Large Magellanic Cloud is a dwarf galaxy orbiting the Milky Way
chapterTaglines.2: Our Milky Way is a barred spiral galaxy
chapterTaglines.3: Hoag's Object is a nearly perfect ring galaxy
chapterTaglines.4: The Virgo Cluster contains over a thousand galaxies
chapterTaglines.5: A prism disperses white light into a spectrum of colors

1: Dwarf galaxies are the most abundant type of galaxy in the universe.
A dwarf galaxy has only a few thousand to billions of stars, while the Milky Way has hundreds.
The Large Magellanic Cloud is 160,000 light-years away, visible to the naked eye in the south.
Supernova SN 1987A erupted in the Large Magellanic Cloud, the closest seen since 1604.
The Tarantula Nebula in the Large Magellanic Cloud is one of the most active nurseries in the Local Group.
Many dwarf galaxies are dominated by dark matter, which cannot be directly seen.
The Small Magellanic Cloud contains hundreds of millions of stars about 200,000 light-years away.
The Magellanic Bridge is a vast stream of gas and stars linking the Large and Small clouds.
The Magellanic Stream is a vast gas trail drawn out by interactions between both clouds and our galaxy.
The Milky Way is orbited by at least fifty dwarf galaxies acting as loyal satellites.
Many dwarf galaxies will eventually be cannibalized and absorbed into our galactic disk.
The Sagittarius Dwarf is currently being torn apart as it plunges through the Milky Way.
Stars in dwarf galaxies are typically metal-poor, closely resembling early generations of stars.
Ultra-faint dwarf galaxies emit so little light that standard telescopes barely detect them.
The Large Magellanic Cloud orbits our galaxy at an astonishing speed of over 300 km per second.
2: The Milky Way is a barred spiral galaxy with hundreds of billions of stars across 100,000 light-years.
Our Solar System resides in the Orion Arm, about 26,000 light-years from the galactic core.
Spiral arms are density waves: stars travel through them rather than remaining trapped.
The Sun takes roughly 230 million years to complete a single orbit around the galactic center.
At the center of our galaxy lies Sagittarius A*, a black hole 4 million times the Sun's mass.
The Andromeda spiral galaxy is predicted to collide with the Milky Way in 4 to 5 billion years.
The central bulge of a spiral galaxy is packed with dense, glowing older yellowish stars.
The galactic halo surrounds the spiral disc, housing globular clusters among the universe's oldest.
The Triangulum Galaxy M33 is the third-largest spiral galaxy in our Local Group.
The Whirlpool Galaxy M51 displays grand-design spiral arms shaped by a nearby companion.
Spiral arms concentrate cold gas and cosmic dust, serving as active stellar nurseries.
Roughly 60% of all galaxies in the nearby universe are spiral galaxies like our own.
The Milky Way's disc is remarkably thin, measuring just 1,000 light-years thick across 100,000.
Most massive spiral galaxies harbor a supermassive black hole anchored at their nucleus.
Our entire Milky Way galaxy hurtles through space at approximately 600 kilometers per second.
3: Ring galaxies typically form when an intruder galaxy punches straight through their center.
Ring galaxies are extraordinarily rare because direct bullseye collisions happen seldom.
Hoag's Object was discovered by astronomer Arthur Hoag in 1950.
Hoag's Object is situated in the Serpens constellation, roughly 600 million light-years away.
The blue outer ring of Hoag's Object hosts young hot stars around an older yellow nucleus.
The precise formation mechanism of Hoag's Object remains actively debated by astronomers.
The Cartwheel Galaxy lies in Sculptor, approximately 500 million light-years from Earth.
Collisional shockwaves compress interstellar gas, igniting bursts of brilliant star birth.
The vibrant ring of the Cartwheel Galaxy expands outward at nearly 90 kilometers per second.
A collision ring lasts only a few hundred million years before gently fading away.
Peering through the gap of Hoag's Object reveals another ring galaxy far in the distance.
The Cartwheel Galaxy features gaseous spokes stretching between its central core and rim.
The Lindsay-Shapley Ring is a classic example of a collisional ring galaxy in our cosmos.
Some ring galaxies arise from internal orbital resonances without any cosmic collision.
A piercing collision sends shock ripples radiating outward like pebbles cast into calm water.
